name: Renal Tubular Transport and Diuretic Pharmacology

reference.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology / Vander's Renal Physiology
clinicalPearls: Proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs 65% of filtered Na+, water and Cl-, and 100% of glucose and amino acids via secondary active transport
Thick ascending limb NKCC2 cotransporter reabsorbs 1 Na+, 1 K+, 2 Cl-; lumen-positive potential (+8 mV) drives paracellular Ca2+ and Mg2+ uptake
Loop diuretics (furosemide) inhibit NKCC2, abolishing medullary osmotic gradient and causing hypercalciuria
Thiazides inhibit distal tubule NCCT cotransporter, promoting Ca2+ reabsorption (protective against calcium nephrolithiasis)
Collecting duct principal cells reabsorb Na+ via ENaC under aldosterone control, generating negative lumen driving K+ and H+ secretion
reference.pathophysiology: Genetic mutations of tubular transporters model diuretic actions: Bartter syndrome mutations (NKCC2, ROMK) mimic loop diuretics with hypokalemic alkalosis and hypercalciuria. Gitelman syndrome mutations (NCCT) mimic thiazides with hypokalemic alkalosis and hypocalciuria. Liddle syndrome gain-of-function ENaC mutations cause pseudoaldosteronism with hypertension and suppressed renin.
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, calcium, magnesium, phosphate
Spot urine electrolytes and fractional excretion of sodium (FENa)
Transtubular potassium gradient (TTKG) and plasma renin/aldosterone ratio
